analysis.one_liner: Guarantees affordable child care for families with children under six and raises child care worker pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new federal entitlement: every child under six whose parents work, study, train, or meet other qualifying conditions could get child care through a private or center-based provider, paid for largely by the federal government. Families below 85 percent of their state's median income would pay nothing, and no family would pay more than 7 percent of income. The bill also requires payment rates high enough to cover providers' real costs and to pay child care staff a living wage equal to what elementary educators with similar credentials earn. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under six, especially low- and middle-income families, would pay little or nothing for child care, with copayments sliding from zero up to a maximum of 7 percent of family income. Children in underserved groups — children with disabilities, homeless children, children in foster care, dual language learners — would be given priority for access. Child care workers would gain a required wage ladder reaching pay equivalent to elementary educators with similar credentials, plus annual cost-of-living increases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young children and child care workers

how_it_helps.text: Creates an entitlement beginning October 1, 2024, under which every eligible child under six is entitled to child care assistance through a grant, contract, or certificate issued directly to the parent.
Families at or below 85 percent of state median income pay no copayment at all, and no family pays more than 7 percent of income toward child care.

Requires state payment rates sufficient to meet providers' full costs of care, including fixed costs, and requires wages for child care staff to be a living wage and equal to what elementary educators with similar credentials and experience earn.

Appropriates $20 billion in fiscal 2024 for grants to localities and Head Start agencies in states that do not take part, plus whatever sums are necessary for fiscal years 2024 through 2029, with the federal government paying 90 percent of direct child care costs.
Prioritizes expanding access and supply for underserved populations, including children with disabilities, infants and toddlers, homeless children, and children in low-income families.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear most of the cost through open-ended mandatory appropriations, with states required to cover at least 10 percent of direct child care costs, maintain their existing child care spending, and pay half of administrative costs. Providers would face new licensing, quality-tier, and wage requirements they would have to meet within set deadlines to stay eligible.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal years 2024 through 2029 on top of the $20 billion startup appropriation, an open-ended mandatory spending commitment rather than a fixed budget.
States must cover at least 10 percent of direct service costs from their own sources and maintain child care spending at their average of the prior three years, which could pressure state budgets.

Providers must meet new licensing, quality-tier, and wage requirements within 2.5 to 4 years of funding, a compliance burden that could push some small or family-based providers out if they cannot make the transition.
Family incomes up to 150 percent of state median and beyond would still owe copayments, so many middle-income families would pay more than nothing even under the expanded program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: near-universal, near-free child care for families with children under six, plus a substantial pay raise for a workforce that is among the lowest paid in education. The cost is large and open-ended, funded by general federal revenue with state matching, and the new quality and licensing requirements create a real transition risk for small family-based providers. The bill is ambitious but spells out financing, matching shares, and timelines in detail; the honest tradeoff is a major new federal entitlement against a major new federal commitment of money.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott introduced the Child Care for Working Families Act on April 27, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
The bill attracted 101 cosponsors, all of them Democrats.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much. Families with young children and child care workers lost a chance at federal help, while taxpayers were spared an open-ended new spending commitment and the child care industry's existing arrangements were left untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; families and workers lost the chance

industries.industry: Child care providers (centers and family child care homes)
industries.note: Federal money would flow through existing private and nonprofit providers as grants, contracts, and parent-held certificates, making them the permanent channel for publicly funded child care while guaranteeing them revenue that covers full costs. In exchange they must meet licensing, quality-tier, and no-suspension requirements and cannot charge families more than the subsidy plus copay.

industries.industry: Early childhood educators and child care staff
industries.note: The bill requires a living wage, a wage ladder tied to credentials, and pay equal to similarly credentialed elementary educators, with at least 70 percent of a separate grant stream spent on personnel costs. This targets one of the lowest-paid workforces in education.

industries.industry: Federal general-revenue taxpayers and higher-income households
industries.note: The program is funded by open-ended federal appropriations with a 90 percent federal share of direct costs, paid from general revenue. Taxpayers as a whole, and wealthier households who pay most federal taxes, would bear the cost.
